prompt: Top K Frequent Elements: return the k most frequent values. Attempt in the checker.
model_answer: Count frequencies in a map, then select the top K. Heap approach: a size-K min-heap by frequency → O(n log K). Even better when counts are bounded: **bucket sort** by frequency (index = count) → O(n). Don't fully sort (O(n log n)). The canonical Top-K problem and a frequent closer.

prompt: Kth Largest Element in an array.
model_answer: Two strong answers: (1) a size-K **min-heap** — push all, keep size K, the root is the Kth largest. O(n log K). (2) **Quickselect** (partition like quicksort but recurse into only one side) — O(n) average, O(1) extra, though O(n²) worst case. Mention both and the trade-off; interviewers often want quickselect for the optimal average bound.

prompt: Merge K sorted linked lists into one sorted list.
model_answer: Min-heap of the K current heads: pop the smallest, append it, push its successor. O(N log K) for N total nodes — far better than concatenating + sorting (O(N log N)) or merging one-by-one (O(NK)). Alternative: divide-and-conquer pairwise merge, also O(N log K). This is the streaming-merge primitive behind external sort and LSM-tree compaction (Step 7).

prompt: Find Median from a Data Stream: support addNum and findMedian as numbers arrive.
model_answer: **Two heaps**: a max-heap for the lower half, a min-heap for the upper half, kept balanced in size (differ by ≤1). The median is the top of the larger heap (or the average of both tops when equal-sized). addNum is O(log n), findMedian O(1). The 'two heaps' technique is a signature hard-interview pattern — recognizing it is the test.
